script.opening: (Gruff, in a hurry, slightly hoarse voice.) "Morning doc. It's probably nothing — I've got a lump on me neck, here on the right. I reckon it's just a gland up from a cold I had a while back. It'll go down on its own, won't it? The wife made me ring. I haven't got time to be poked about, the pub doesn't run itself. Can you just tell me it's nothing to worry about?"

facts.text: Right side of the neck, under the angle of the jaw. "Five weeks, maybe. It hasn't gone down. If anything it's a bit bigger. Doesn't hurt though. Feels hard." Can point to it on camera — the doctor may see a visible swelling. The cold was about six weeks ago and settled in a few days.

If asked: "Now you mention it, it's been a bit rough for a few weeks. I put it down to shouting last orders." Throat feels raw on the right. If asked: no trouble swallowing, food doesn't stick, no earache, no mouth ulcers or patches he has seen, no coughing blood.
If asked: no night sweats, no fevers, no itch. "Not that I've noticed" to weight loss — trousers no different. Appetite fine. No other lumps in armpits or groin.

"About twenty a day, since I was a lad" (about 25 pack-years). Drink: "More than I should. Comes with the job" — 4–5 pints most nights plus whisky at weekends (around 60–70 units a week). No early-morning drinking or shakes. Never tried to stop smoking.
Rarely sees a doctor. No known illnesses, no regular medicines, no allergies.
Self-employed publican, runs the pub with his wife, Sue. "No work, no money. And I don't do doctors. Never have."
If asked what he is worried about: his dad died of throat cancer in his sixties — "he smoked like a chimney too".

Gruff and impatient; minimise everything. Admit the hoarse voice if asked. If asked what worries him, pause: "Same as me dad, probably. Cancer. With the smoking. I'd rather not know, if I'm honest." If the doctor says it's just a gland, agree quickly and try to leave. If the doctor is straight but calm, ask "When?" and accept: "The wife can run it for a day or two." Lukewarm about stopping smoking: "Maybe. Let me get this sorted first."

ice.ideas: "Just a gland up from a cold. It'll go down."
ice.concerns: HIDDEN AGENDA — his dad died of throat cancer and he smokes and drinks the same way. He has noticed the voice and that the lump is growing and is scared, but would rather not know. Worried about the pub and money if he's ill.
ice.expectations: "Tell me it's nothing — and no poking about."

cues: "The wife made me ring." — someone else is worried; why?
"Put it down to shouting last orders." — the hoarse voice, played down.
"I'd rather not know." — the fear, if invited.

checkpoints.text: Recognises a neck lump persisting beyond ~3–4 weeks as UNEXPLAINED (a reactive gland should settle) and does not accept "just a gland from a cold" — characterising it and ELICITING the downplayed hoarseness, throat symptoms, smoking and alcohol

Identifies the HIGH-RISK head & neck profile (smoker + heavy alcohol + persistent neck lump + hoarseness) and screens lymphoma B symptoms (night sweats, weight loss, fevers, itch, generalised lymphadenopathy)

EXAMINES face to face (not possible on video) the neck lump, oral cavity/oropharynx, thyroid and regional nodes (and looks for hepatosplenomegaly/other nodes), characterising the lump (site, size, consistency, fixity)

Applies NICE NG12: refers on the head and neck SUSPECTED CANCER PATHWAY for an unexplained neck lump/persistent hoarseness at 45+ (laryngeal; oral for a persistent unexplained neck lump; thyroid if a thyroid lump), considers lymphoma, arranges an FBC as a baseline, and a CHEST X-RAY because he is 40+ with persistent cervical lymphadenopathy

Addresses the modifiable risk — offers smoking cessation and alcohol brief intervention — without lecturing, and considers the broader differential (reactive, haematological, thyroid, benign) rather than labelling it benign from the chair
Reads the "no time / tell me it’s nothing" as avoidance, treats the wife’s push as the reliable signal, surfaces the worry gently and does NOT collude with the wish to be reassured
Balances honesty (a lump this persistent, with your background, needs urgent checking) with calm reassurance so a reluctant man engages with examination and referral

Safety-nets and follows up: the suspected cancer pathway and what to expect, FBC/CXR results, red flags warranting sooner review, cessation/alcohol support, confirms he will attend, and reviews the outcome — examination + correct NICE NG12 referral, not "it’ll go down on its own"

worked.txt: "I’m glad your wife nudged you — and I’m not going to just tell you it’s a gland over a video call, because a gland from a cold goes down in a couple of weeks, and yours has been there over a month and isn’t shifting. That earns a proper look, not a brush-off."

"Few quick questions. Has your voice been husky or hoarse at all? … A few weeks, yes. Any soreness swallowing? And the smoking — how much, and how’s the drink? … Thank you for being straight with me; that all matters and it’s exactly why I asked rather than assumed."

"I’ll be honest with you, because I think you’d want that. A lump in the neck that’s hung around, with a hoarse voice, in someone who smokes and drinks a fair bit — that’s a combination I need a specialist to check quickly. It can be a problem in the voice box or throat. I’m not telling you it IS — but it has to be ruled out fast."

"I need to examine your neck, mouth, throat and your thyroid in person, and feel for other glands — I can’t do that on video, so can you come in today? I’m going to arrange a blood count and a chest X-ray too, because a neck gland that has stayed this long at your age needs a chest X-ray, and the blood count helps me cover the other possible causes."

"Given all of it together, I’m referring you on the urgent suspected cancer pathway to the head-and-neck specialists — you’ll be seen quickly. That’s the safe, right step, and getting it looked at fast is exactly what gives the best outcome whatever it turns out to be."

"I’m not here to give you a hard time about the fags and the pints — but cutting down would genuinely help, and I can support that whenever you’re ready. If the lump grows, the voice worsens, or you feel unwell before the appointment, contact us sooner. I’ll chase the bloods and X-ray and make sure that referral goes today."

f.learning: A neck lump persisting beyond about 3–4 weeks is UNEXPLAINED — a reactive node from a cold settles within 2–3 weeks — and must be taken seriously, examined and routed, not assumed to be a post-viral "gland". The examinable danger here is the HIGH-RISK head & neck profile: a heavy smoker and drinker (synergistic risk factors for head & neck squamous cell cancer) with a persistent neck lump PLUS a few weeks of hoarseness/throat discomfort. NICE NG12 (Suspected cancer: recognition and referral, last updated April 2026): consider a suspected cancer pathway referral for laryngeal cancer in people aged 45 and over with persistent unexplained hoarseness OR an unexplained lump in the neck; consider one for oral cancer (persistent unexplained neck lump) and thyroid cancer (unexplained thyroid lump); consider one for lymphoma with unexplained lymphadenopathy, taking B symptoms and alcohol-induced node pain into account (an FBC is a baseline, not the NG12 route); and consider an urgent chest X-ray at 40 and over with persistent cervical lymphadenopathy (lung). Arrange a face-to-face examination of the neck, mouth, oropharynx and thyroid; screen the broader differential (reactive, haematological, thyroid, benign) rather than labelling it benign from the chair; and address smoking and alcohol with brief intervention, not a lecture. The hidden agenda is avoidance — a self-employed man who never attends, doesn’t want to lose the business or hear bad news, minimising a lump and a hoarse voice he has half-noticed, with the spouse’s push the reliable signal. Elicit the downplayed symptoms, refer urgently with honesty but no panic, support the risk factors, and safety-net and follow up.

knowledge.guideline: NICE NG209 (tobacco, 2021) · NICE NG12 Suspected cancer: recognition and referral (2015, last updated 15 April 2026) · NICE PH24 (alcohol brief interventions, 2010) · NICE CG115 (alcohol dependence, 2011)
knowledge.summary: A neck lump that has not settled after several weeks is unexplained. In a smoker and heavy drinker aged 49 with hoarseness, it goes on a head and neck suspected cancer pathway referral.

points.t: NICE NG12: consider a suspected cancer pathway referral for laryngeal cancer in people aged 45 and over with persistent unexplained hoarseness or an unexplained lump in the neck. Consider one for oral cancer with a persistent and unexplained lump in the neck. He meets both on two counts.
NICE NG12: consider a suspected cancer pathway referral for thyroid cancer in people with an unexplained thyroid lump. Examination decides whether the lump is thyroid or nodal.

NICE NG12: consider a suspected cancer pathway referral for Hodgkin lymphoma in adults with unexplained lymphadenopathy, taking into account fever, night sweats, shortness of breath, pruritus, weight loss or alcohol-induced lymph node pain; for non-Hodgkin lymphoma, unexplained lymphadenopathy or splenomegaly, taking into account the same symptoms except alcohol-induced pain. An FBC is a reasonable clinical baseline, not an NICE NG12 requirement.

NICE NG12: consider an urgent direct-access chest X-ray (within 2 weeks) to assess for lung cancer in people aged 40 and over with persistent cervical lymphadenopathy (or supraclavicular lymphadenopathy, persistent or recurrent chest infection, finger clubbing, chest signs consistent with lung cancer or thrombocytosis). At 49 with a persistent neck node he meets it whatever his smoking history; the 25 pack-years add to the concern.

Smoking and alcohol multiply each other’s risk for head and neck cancer. Offer very brief advice and referral to stop-smoking support (NICE NG209) and an alcohol brief intervention using AUDIT (NICE PH24), without delaying the referral.
If he is alcohol-dependent, sudden cessation risks withdrawal seizures and delirium; planned withdrawal is needed (NICE CG115). Ask before advising him to stop.

dg.d: Open start; let him make his case for “just a gland” before narrowing.
Self-employed publican, no sick pay, avoids doctors; smoking and alcohol quantified without judgement.
Face-to-face exam of neck, mouth, oropharynx, thyroid and other node sites; FBC; chest X-ray.
Head and neck cancer, lymphoma, thyroid, reactive node, benign lumps; asked about B symptoms and alcohol-induced node pain.
Asked about dysphagia, mouth ulcers, earache and weight loss; gave airway red flags.
Persistent unexplained neck lump with hoarseness at 49 meeting NICE NG12 head and neck criteria.
After open exploration, used closed questions with clear signposting to confirm specific details.
Used information already available in the notes/referral; did not re-ask what was already documented or said.

dg.t: Finishes data gathering in good time
dg.d: History, ICE, psychosocial context and red-flag screen completed by ~6–7 minutes, leaving time for explanation and a shared plan.

cm.d: Head and neck suspected cancer pathway referral today, exam, FBC and CXR, planned around the pub.
Very brief advice on smoking with an offer of support; alcohol brief intervention; screened for dependence and warned against abrupt stopping.
Chase if no date in a week; same-day and 999 symptoms; GP reviews results with him.

cm.t: Uses psychosocial information in the plan
cm.d: Tailored the plan to the patient’s circumstances, beliefs and practical barriers rather than giving a generic plan.

cm.t: Shares risks and safety of options
cm.d: Explained the benefits and risks of the options clearly, as concrete terms or numbers where possible.
Acknowledged autonomy, capacity, confidentiality, safeguarding and any fitness-to-drive/work or duty-of-care implications relevant to this case.
Moved efficiently through the consultation so all key areas were covered within the time without getting stuck.

ro.d: Picked up the wife’s push and the downplayed hoarse voice, and explored both.
Idea (a post-viral gland), concern (cancer, losing the business), expectation (to be told it is nothing).
Warm, non-judgmental tone; put the patient at ease and showed respect for their perspective.
Opened broadly and let the patient tell their story before narrowing down.
When a cue was offered, stopped and explored the specific concern rather than reassuring superficially and moving on.
Active listening throughout — reflecting, pausing, not interrupting — interested in the patient as a person.
Told the patient why a question, examination or test was being done — transparent reasoning throughout.
Explained the working diagnosis or analysis in plain language the patient could understand.

ro.t: Shares and uses ICE in the plan

He has noticed the voice and that the lump is growing and is scared, but would rather not know. Worried about the pub and money if he's ill — directly within the plan, rather than noting it and moving on.
Checked understanding, offered written/follow-up support, asked if anything else was on their mind, agreed next steps.
Clear agenda set early, logical flow from data gathering to management. Did not jump to a plan before gathering enough information.
Explained clinical terms in plain English, or defined them immediately; checked the patient was following.
Noticed and responded to emotional and verbal cues rather than continuing a fixed clinical script.

model.text: Morning Derek, I’m Dr Hughes. What can I do for you?
model.why: Open start

model.text: It’s probably nothing. I’ve got a lump on me neck, here on the right. Just a gland up from a cold, I reckon. The wife made me ring. I haven’t got time to be poked about — can you just tell me it’s nothing?
I’m glad she did. I’ll be quick and straight with you. I want to ask a few questions, tell you what I think, and agree what we do. Fair?
model.why: Brief agenda suited to a reluctant attender

model.text: Go on then.
How long has it been there, and has it changed?
model.why: Duration and growth

model.text: Five weeks, maybe. It hasn’t gone down. If anything it’s a bit bigger. Doesn’t hurt though. Feels hard.
A gland from a cold usually settles within a couple of weeks, so one that’s been there five weeks and grown is one I need to look into. Has your voice changed at all — husky or hoarse?
model.why: Rejects “just a gland”; elicits hoarseness

model.text: Now you mention it, it’s been a bit rough for a few weeks. I put it down to shouting last orders. Throat’s been a bit uncomfortable too.
Any trouble swallowing, ulcers in your mouth that won’t heal, or earache on that side?
model.why: Head and neck red flags

model.text: Not really. Just the throat feeling a bit raw.
Have you had night sweats, fevers, itching, lost weight without trying, or any pain in the lump after a drink?
model.why: Lymphoma features including alcohol-induced node pain

model.text: Not that I’ve noticed.
Your notes say you smoke. How much now? And how much do you drink in a typical week — honestly, I’m not here to judge.
model.why: Quantifies the key risk factors non-judgementally

model.text: About twenty a day, since I was a lad. Drink — more than I should. Comes with the job.
Thank you for being straight. If you went a day without a drink, would you get shaky or sweaty?
model.why: Screens for dependence before advising change

model.text: Never tried, to be honest.
You said you haven’t time to be poked about. What would it mean for you if this needed hospital tests?
model.why: Explores the avoidance and its reasons

model.text: The pub doesn’t run itself. I’m self-employed — no work, no money. And I don’t do doctors. Never have.
That’s a real pressure. And your wife pushing you to ring — what do you think she’s worried about?
model.why: Uses the spouse’s push to surface the unspoken fear

model.text: (Pause.) Same as me, probably. Cancer. With the smoking. I’d rather not know, if I’m honest.
I understand that. But not knowing doesn’t change what it is — it only changes how early we can act. And early is what matters most.
model.why: Acknowledges fear; declines to collude

model.text: Here’s my honest view. A lump that’s stayed five weeks, a hoarse voice for weeks, and twenty a day with a fair bit of drink — that’s a combination I can’t call a gland. It could be something in the voice box or throat, and it needs a specialist to check quickly.
model.why: Names the high-risk picture honestly

model.text: So it is cancer.

I don’t know that, and you don’t either. There are other causes — infections, the thyroid gland, harmless lumps. But the guidance for someone your age with these symptoms is an urgent suspected cancer pathway referral to the ear, nose and throat team — you should be seen quickly and get an answer within 4 weeks (28 days).
model.why: Holds the differential; applies NICE NG12

model.text: I also need to examine you in person — your neck, your mouth and throat, your thyroid, and other glands. And I’d like a blood count and a chest X-ray, because a neck gland can sometimes come from the chest or the blood.
model.why: Face-to-face exam; FBC as a clinical baseline and CXR per NICE NG12 (40 and over with persistent cervical lymphadenopathy)

model.text: When?
Can you come in today? It’s ten minutes. I’ll send the referral today whatever I find, and the blood test and X-ray can be done this week. What cover can you get for the pub?
model.why: Plans around his business

model.text: The wife can run it for a day or two. She’ll be glad I’m doing something.

On the smoking and the drink — this isn’t a lecture. Stopping smoking now genuinely helps whatever this turns out to be, and there’s free support that doubles your chances. Would you like me to refer you?
model.why: Very brief advice and offer of support

model.text: Maybe. Let me get this sorted first.
Fair enough — I’ll put the offer in writing. Please don’t suddenly stop drinking altogether without talking to us first, because that can make you unwell. We’ll look at cutting down safely together.
model.why: Safe alcohol advice; respects his pace

model.text: If you haven’t heard from the hospital within a week, ring us. If you struggle to swallow, your breathing gets noisy or difficult, or you cough up blood, get seen that day — and for breathing trouble, call 999.
model.why: Specific red flags, including airway

model.text: What will you tell your wife tonight?
model.why: Teach-back using his own frame

model.text: That it’s not just a gland, I’m being checked quick by the throat people, bloods and an X-ray, and I’ll think about the fags.
Spot on. I’ll see you this afternoon and I’ll go through the results with you. You did the right thing ringing.
model.why: Ownership of follow-up; affirms

social.t: Self-employed people are not entitled to Statutory Sick Pay. If investigations or treatment stop him working, he may be able to claim New Style Employment and Support Allowance or Universal Credit; Citizens Advice can help.
Running a pub normalises heavy drinking and makes cutting down harder. Acknowledge this rather than moralise.

legal.t: If he declined referral, he is entitled to, provided he has capacity. Explain the risks clearly, record it, and keep the offer open.

professional.t: GMC Good medical practice (2024): be honest and give patients the information they need. Reassuring him to keep him happy would be unsafe.
Track suspected cancer referrals and pending FBC and CXR results so none are lost, especially in a patient likely to disengage.

community.t: Local NHS stop-smoking service; community alcohol services; Macmillan Cancer Support if a diagnosis is made.

redFlags: Neck lump persisting beyond a few weeks, hard and enlarging
Dysphagia, stridor, haemoptysis, weight loss, night sweats
psychosocial: Self-employed publican — no sick pay, fears for the business
Smoking 20 a day and heavy drinking; screen for dependence
Avoids doctors; wife prompted the call
ice: Idea: “Just a gland up from a cold”
Concern: cancer, and the pub going under
Expectation: to be told it is nothing without being examined

playbook.diagnosis: Persistent unexplained right neck lump with several weeks of hoarseness in a 49-year-old smoker and heavy drinker: meets NICE NG12 criteria for a head and neck suspected cancer pathway referral. Differential includes lymphoma, thyroid, reactive and benign causes.
playbook.diagnosisLay: “A gland from a cold goes down in a couple of weeks. Yours hasn’t, and with the hoarse voice and the smoking, I need a throat specialist to check it quickly. It might be something simple, but we need to know.”

management.reflectIce: “You said you’d rather not know. I get that. But knowing early is what gives you the most options — and it’s what your wife was hoping for too.”
management.psychosocial: Plan cover for the pub; offer smoking and alcohol support at his pace; signpost benefits advice if work stops.
sharedPlan: Head and neck suspected cancer pathway referral today
Face-to-face exam of neck, mouth, throat and thyroid today
FBC and chest X-ray this week
Very brief advice on smoking; alcohol brief intervention; no abrupt stopping
safetyNet: Trouble swallowing or coughing blood — same-day review
Ring if no appointment within a week; GP reviews results

pitfalls.intro: This station is failed by accepting the patient’s explanation. The lump, the voice and the risk factors together are the test; the reluctant man is the communication challenge.

items.fail: Accepting “a gland from a cold” and reviewing in a few weeks, or giving antibiotics.
items.why: NICE NG12: an unexplained lump in the neck at 45 or over means considering a laryngeal suspected cancer pathway referral (and a persistent unexplained neck lump at any age, one for oral cancer). A persistent lump is not reactive by default.
items.fix: State the time course — a reactive gland settles in weeks — and refer.

items.fail: Not asking about the voice, swallowing or mouth, so the hoarseness is missed.
items.why: He will not volunteer it. Persistent hoarseness at 45 or over is itself an NICE NG12 criterion.
items.fix: Ask directly about voice, swallowing, ulcers and earache.

items.fail: Referring but forgetting the FBC and chest X-ray.
items.why: Neck nodes can reflect lymphoma or lung disease; NICE NG12 advises considering an urgent CXR at 40 or over with persistent cervical lymphadenopathy.
items.fix: Add FBC and CXR, and explain why in plain words.

items.fail: A lecture on smoking and alcohol that makes him defensive.
items.why: Judgemental delivery loses the patient and Relating marks.
items.fix: Very brief advice, an offer of support, and respect for his timing.

items.fail: Missing the fear behind “no time” and “the wife made me”.
items.why: Avoidance is the hidden agenda; unaddressed, he may not attend.
items.fix: “What do you think she’s worried about?” — then answer that fear honestly.

items.fail: Advising him to stop drinking immediately.
items.why: If he is dependent, abrupt stopping risks withdrawal seizures (NICE CG115).
items.fix: Screen for dependence first; plan any reduction safely.

timeMap.d: He wants a quick “it’s nothing”. Keep the agenda short and business-like.
Duration, growth, hardness, hoarseness, swallowing, mouth ulcers, earache, B symptoms, smoking, alcohol and dependence.
Use the wife’s push to surface the fear of cancer and of losing the pub.
Name the high-risk combination, refer on the head and neck pathway, exam in person today, FBC and CXR, offer smoking and alcohol support.
Chase if no date, airway and swallowing red flags, teach-back, results reviewed.

wordPics.fail: Accepts “a gland from a cold”, offers antibiotics or review in a month; never asks about the voice; lectures on smoking and drinking; no referral.
wordPics.pass: Recognises a persistent unexplained neck lump, finds the hoarseness, refers on the NICE NG12 head and neck pathway, arranges an in-person exam and gives a safety-net.
wordPics.exc: All of that, plus: surfaces the fear through the wife’s push; adds FBC and CXR with reasons; offers smoking and alcohol support without a lecture and checks dependence; plans around the pub; teach-back and owned follow-up.

avoid.instead: “A gland from a cold settles in a couple of weeks. Five weeks and growing needs a specialist to look.”
avoid.why: Delaying a persistent unexplained neck lump in a high-risk man is the core Tasks fail.

avoid.dont: “You really need to stop smoking and drinking right now.”
avoid.instead: “Stopping smoking helps whatever this turns out to be — want me to set up support? And don’t stop drinking suddenly without talking to us.”
avoid.why: A lecture loses him; abrupt alcohol withdrawal can be dangerous.

avoid.instead: “This combination needs checking quickly to rule out a problem in the voice box or throat.”

Can you come in today? It’s ten minutes. I’ll send the referral today whatever I find, and the blood test and X-ray can be done this week. What cover can you get for the pub?

On the smoking and the drink — this isn’t a lecture. Stopping smoking now genuinely helps whatever this turns out to be, and there’s free support that doubles your chances. Would you like me to refer you?

SCA_MODELS.text: Maybe. Let me get this sorted first.
Fair enough — I’ll put the offer in writing. Please don’t suddenly stop drinking altogether without talking to us first, because that can make you unwell. We’ll look at cutting down safely together.

SCA_MODELS.text: If you haven’t heard from the hospital within a week, ring us. If you struggle to swallow, your breathing gets noisy or difficult, or you cough up blood, get seen that day — and for breathing trouble, call 999.

SCA_STEM.name: Derek Mahoney
SCA_STEM.recent: Rarely attends. Self-employed publican. Appointment booked by his wife: “lump in neck”.
SCA_STEM.reason: Lump on the right side of his neck for about 5 weeks.

SCA_KNOWLEDGE.guideline: NICE NG209 (tobacco, 2021) · NICE NG12 Suspected cancer: recognition and referral (2015, last updated 15 April 2026) · NICE PH24 (alcohol brief interventions, 2010) · NICE CG115 (alcohol dependence, 2011)
SCA_KNOWLEDGE.summary: A neck lump that has not settled after several weeks is unexplained. In a smoker and heavy drinker aged 49 with hoarseness, it goes on a head and neck suspected cancer pathway referral.

points.t: NICE NG12: consider a suspected cancer pathway referral for laryngeal cancer in people aged 45 and over with persistent unexplained hoarseness or an unexplained lump in the neck. Consider one for oral cancer with a persistent and unexplained lump in the neck. He meets both on two counts.
NICE NG12: consider a suspected cancer pathway referral for thyroid cancer in people with an unexplained thyroid lump. Examination decides whether the lump is thyroid or nodal.

NICE NG12: consider a suspected cancer pathway referral for Hodgkin lymphoma in adults with unexplained lymphadenopathy, taking into account fever, night sweats, shortness of breath, pruritus, weight loss or alcohol-induced lymph node pain; for non-Hodgkin lymphoma, unexplained lymphadenopathy or splenomegaly, taking into account the same symptoms except alcohol-induced pain. An FBC is a reasonable clinical baseline, not an NICE NG12 requirement.

NICE NG12: consider an urgent direct-access chest X-ray (within 2 weeks) to assess for lung cancer in people aged 40 and over with persistent cervical lymphadenopathy (or supraclavicular lymphadenopathy, persistent or recurrent chest infection, finger clubbing, chest signs consistent with lung cancer or thrombocytosis). At 49 with a persistent neck node he meets it whatever his smoking history; the 25 pack-years add to the concern.

Smoking and alcohol multiply each other’s risk for head and neck cancer. Offer very brief advice and referral to stop-smoking support (NICE NG209) and an alcohol brief intervention using AUDIT (NICE PH24), without delaying the referral.
If he is alcohol-dependent, sudden cessation risks withdrawal seizures and delirium; planned withdrawal is needed (NICE CG115). Ask before advising him to stop.

SCA_SC_TASKS.d: Open start; let him make his case for “just a gland” before narrowing.
Self-employed publican, no sick pay, avoids doctors; smoking and alcohol quantified without judgement.
Picked up the wife’s push and the downplayed hoarse voice, and explored both.
Idea (a post-viral gland), concern (cancer, losing the business), expectation (to be told it is nothing).
Face-to-face exam of neck, mouth, oropharynx, thyroid and other node sites; FBC; chest X-ray.
Head and neck cancer, lymphoma, thyroid, reactive node, benign lumps; asked about B symptoms and alcohol-induced node pain.
Asked about dysphagia, mouth ulcers, earache and weight loss; gave airway red flags.
Persistent unexplained neck lump with hoarseness at 49 meeting NICE NG12 head and neck criteria.
Head and neck suspected cancer pathway referral today, exam, FBC and CXR, planned around the pub.
Very brief advice on smoking with an offer of support; alcohol brief intervention; screened for dependence and warned against abrupt stopping.
Chase if no date in a week; same-day and 999 symptoms; GP reviews results with him.

social.t: Self-employed people are not entitled to Statutory Sick Pay. If investigations or treatment stop him working, he may be able to claim New Style Employment and Support Allowance or Universal Credit; Citizens Advice can help.
Running a pub normalises heavy drinking and makes cutting down harder. Acknowledge this rather than moralise.

legal.t: If he declined referral, he is entitled to, provided he has capacity. Explain the risks clearly, record it, and keep the offer open.

professional.t: GMC Good medical practice (2024): be honest and give patients the information they need. Reassuring him to keep him happy would be unsafe.
Track suspected cancer referrals and pending FBC and CXR results so none are lost, especially in a patient likely to disengage.

community.t: Local NHS stop-smoking service; community alcohol services; Macmillan Cancer Support if a diagnosis is made.

redFlags: Neck lump persisting beyond a few weeks, hard and enlarging
Dysphagia, stridor, haemoptysis, weight loss, night sweats
psychosocial: Self-employed publican — no sick pay, fears for the business
Smoking 20 a day and heavy drinking; screen for dependence
Avoids doctors; wife prompted the call
ice: Idea: “Just a gland up from a cold”
Concern: cancer, and the pub going under
Expectation: to be told it is nothing without being examined

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: Persistent unexplained right neck lump with several weeks of hoarseness in a 49-year-old smoker and heavy drinker: meets NICE NG12 criteria for a head and neck suspected cancer pathway referral. Differential includes lymphoma, thyroid, reactive and benign causes.
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: “A gland from a cold goes down in a couple of weeks. Yours hasn’t, and with the hoarse voice and the smoking, I need a throat specialist to check it quickly. It might be something simple, but we need to know.”

management.reflectIce: “You said you’d rather not know. I get that. But knowing early is what gives you the most options — and it’s what your wife was hoping for too.”
management.psychosocial: Plan cover for the pub; offer smoking and alcohol support at his pace; signpost benefits advice if work stops.

FBC and chest X-ray this week

safetyNet: Trouble swallowing or coughing blood — same-day review

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: This station is failed by accepting the patient’s explanation. The lump, the voice and the risk factors together are the test; the reluctant man is the communication challenge.

items.fail: Accepting “a gland from a cold” and reviewing in a few weeks, or giving antibiotics.
items.why: NICE NG12: an unexplained lump in the neck at 45 or over means considering a laryngeal suspected cancer pathway referral (and a persistent unexplained neck lump at any age, one for oral cancer). A persistent lump is not reactive by default.
items.fix: State the time course — a reactive gland settles in weeks — and refer.

items.fail: Not asking about the voice, swallowing or mouth, so the hoarseness is missed.
items.why: He will not volunteer it. Persistent hoarseness at 45 or over is itself an NICE NG12 criterion.
items.fix: Ask directly about voice, swallowing, ulcers and earache.

items.fail: Referring but forgetting the FBC and chest X-ray.
items.why: Neck nodes can reflect lymphoma or lung disease; NICE NG12 advises considering an urgent CXR at 40 or over with persistent cervical lymphadenopathy.
items.fix: Add FBC and CXR, and explain why in plain words.

items.fail: A lecture on smoking and alcohol that makes him defensive.
items.why: Judgemental delivery loses the patient and Relating marks.
items.fix: Very brief advice, an offer of support, and respect for his timing.

items.fail: Missing the fear behind “no time” and “the wife made me”.
items.why: Avoidance is the hidden agenda; unaddressed, he may not attend.
items.fix: “What do you think she’s worried about?” — then answer that fear honestly.

items.fail: Advising him to stop drinking immediately.
items.why: If he is dependent, abrupt stopping risks withdrawal seizures (NICE CG115).
items.fix: Screen for dependence first; plan any reduction safely.
